`verifyNoteUpdate` selects `events[0]` when multiple `NoteUpdated` logs exist in the same tx. Since the DB schema is idempotent on `(chainId, txHash)`, persisting an arbitrary event can record the wrong note if a transaction emits multiple updates. Consider rejecting transactions with 0 or >1 matching events to avoid ambiguous persistence.

`verifySettlement` uses `events.find(...)` and assumes at most one matching `Subscribed` event per transaction. file.content:
name: CI

on:
  push:
  pull_request:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  contracts:
    name: Contracts (Foundry)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: packages/contracts
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: recursive

      - name: Install Foundry
        uses: foundry-rs/foundry-toolchain@v1

      # The ERC-3643/ONCHAINID/OpenZeppelin libraries are npm deps resolved through
      # foundry.toml remappings into node_modules (not git submodules), so forge build/test
      # need the workspace installed first.
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 10

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm

      - name: Install dependencies
        working-directory: ${{ github.workspace }}
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Check formatting
        run: forge fmt --check

      - name: Build
        run: forge build --sizes

      - name: Test
        run: forge test -vvv

  web:
    name: Web (Next.js)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 10

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Typecheck
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web typecheck

      - name: Lint
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web lint

      - name: Test
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web test

      - name: Build
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web build

The vendored T-REX/ONCHAINID files pin **exact `0.8.17`**, so any of our files that import them (or are imported by a 0.8.17 file) are locked to 0.8.17 too — we can't float those, and we won't touch the audited T-REX code. A floor of `^0.8.28` accepts both your `0.8.35` nightly and Foundry's downloaded `0.8.28`. Let me find all the standalone (non-T-REX) files and relax those:

## What & why

Implements **BRD Epic 4 — Primary Subscription & Settlement (atomic DvP)** for issue #3. A Subscriber buys Fraction Tokens in a primary offering paying a **mock regulated stablecoin**, settled as **atomic delivery-versus-payment**: stablecoin → Vendor and freshly minted ERC-3643 Fraction Tokens → Subscriber in one transaction, or the whole thing reverts.

Built Ctrl Alt-independent behind mock-as-interface seams (ADR-0004, ADR-0005).

> **Note — this PR is stacked on issue #2.** Issue #2 (ERC-3643 identity, mock KYC claim & on-chain whitelist) was never merged to `main`, so its commit rides along here under `feat/...-issue-3`. That is why the diff also contains the identity suite, the mock KYC claim issuer / endpoint, and the walking-skeleton scaffolding.

## Mocks in R1 (what is mocked vs production-realistic)

Per CLAUDE.md "Mocks & how to replace them", every Ctrl Alt capability is mocked behind the interface its real counterpart will expose:

| Capability | R1 mock | Tracking issue |
|---|---|---|
| KYC + claim issuer (Ctrl Alt) | mock KYC endpoint + ERC-3643 trusted issuer — **from #2, already accepted** | #11 |
| Stablecoin + fiat on/off-ramp (Ctrl Alt) | `MockStablecoin` (ERC-20 + faucet) — **new in this PR** | #12 |

The on-chain verification/settlement paths are real ERC-3643; only the off-chain provider decisions are mocked. Replacement is an integration swap, not a rewrite.

## Contracts (`packages/contracts`)

- **`MockStablecoin`** — ERC-20 cash leg (6dp) with an open faucet simulating the fiat on-ramp (Ctrl Alt seam #12). The DvP contract depends only on `IERC20`, never on the mock.
- **`PrimaryOffering`** — atomic DvP. Per-cell offering params (unit price, discount, optional platform fee, total cap, per-investor limit). `subscribe()` pulls stablecoin to the Vendor (+ fee to the fee recipient) and mints Fraction Tokens to the caller; the ERC-3643 compliance check on the delivery leg reverts (unwinding the cash leg) when the buyer isn't whitelisted/verified or is frozen. CEI + `ReentrancyGuard`. Emits `Subscribed` + `ProceedsReleased` for reconciliation (FR4.3).
- **`DeployOffering.s.sol`** — deploys the rail, grants the offering the token agent role so it can mint, and creates a demo offering.

## Web (`apps/web`)

- Settlement **read-model** in Neon (+ in-memory fallback) behind one interface; pure **cost-basis aggregation** (`aggregateHoldings`, test-first).
- **`/api/portfolio`** — record a confirmed settlement; return holdings + history. Writes are gated by a server-side **on-chain trust boundary** (`lib/portfolio/verify.ts`): the row is re-derived from the on-chain `Subscribed` event, not from client input. The Register read-model (`/api/records`) uses the same pattern (`lib/records/verify.ts`).
- **`SubscriptionPanel`** — live price/discount/fees/balance, approve + DvP confirm (FR4.5).
- **`Portfolio`** — holdings, cost basis, settlement history (FR4.6).

## Acceptance criteria (issue #3)

- [x] Mock stablecoin + DvP subscription contract; buy is atomic (token+cash or revert), tested
- [x] Per-cell offering parameters (price/discount, caps, limits) enforced
- [x] Vendor receives proceeds on settlement
- [x] Subscription UI shows price/discount/fees/balance and confirms DvP
- [x] Portfolio reflects holdings + cost basis; settlement events emitted

## Deferred (out of scope, noted in code)

- Escrowed/conditional settlement + fiat-wire fallback leg (FR4.2/FR4.8) → governance windows, Epic 7.
- Real Ctrl Alt stablecoin + fiat on/off-ramp + reconciliation webhooks → **#12**. Real Ctrl Alt KYC → **#11**.

## Tests

- **Foundry: 28 pass** (14 new in `PrimaryOffering.t.sol`, against a real ERC-3643 suite): atomic happy path, revert unwinds cash on failed delivery (non-whitelisted / insufficient balance), cap & per-investor enforcement, discount/fee math, access control, fuzz.
- **Web: 18 pass** (cost-basis aggregation + settlements/records repos incl. idempotency). Typecheck + lint + `next build` + `forge fmt --check` clean.

Closes #3.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.thinking:
Looking at the security feedback from round 7, there's a valid concern about the KYC endpoint signing transactions with the server key without proper guards. I need to add a production safety check—something like an environment flag that explicitly allows this behavior, so it won't accidentally run in production without intentional configuration.

The key insight is that `/api/portfolio` and `/api/records` don't have the same risk since they only read and persist verified data without spending gas. The KYC endpoint is the one that needs gating. I'll add a guard that blocks the mock KYC in production unless `ENABLE_MOCK_KYC=true` is explicitly set, forcing the operator to opt in intentionally.

For the SubscriptionPanel issue with `Number(offeringId)` losing precision on bigints, I'm considering whether to send it as a string instead and have the API parse it. The cleanest approach is to accept `offeringId` as either a string or number in the API, then convert it safely to BigInt throughout the chain — this way the SettlementClaim can store it as a string and avoid precision loss entirely.

But this cascades: the database schema has `offering_id` as BIGINT, and the SettlementRecord type currently expects a number. Since offering IDs in practice are small sequential integers, the real risk is minimal. However, the reviewer wants correctness, so the pragmatic fix is to add a safe-integer guard on the client before converting the bigint to a number, and rely on the server-side validation that already checks `isSafeInteger` — if the client sends an unsafe number, the server rejects it anyway.

Actually, the cleanest approach is to switch the entire API to use strings for `offeringId` end-to-end. This avoids the bigint-to-number conversion entirely. I'll update the SettlementClaim type to accept `offeringId` as a string, validate it server-side with a regex check for digits, then convert to BigInt for verification logic while storing the numeric value in the database record. Adding the safe-integer guard in the effect...

For the pricing duplication, I should switch from the client-side `priceFor()` calculation to reading the contract's `quote()` function directly via `useReadContract`, passing the offering ID and quantity to get authoritative net, fee, and total values. This means replacing the local pricing logic with an RPC call that updates whenever quantity changes, which is fine for the demo.

The quote function returns zeros when quantity is 0, so I'll only enable the read when quantity is greater than 0. Before the async read completes, cost will be undefined and buttons stay disabled. I'm setting up the hook to destructure the tuple response into the cost object...

Now I need to remove the priceFor function and the BPS constant since they're no longer needed.

For the DeployOffering script, I'll add an environment variable for the fee recipient that defaults to the deployer, then use it when feeBps is greater than 0.

I'm tackling these in order: the contract fix first, then the KYC route, then the SubscriptionPanel changes together. Let me start by checking the DeployOffering script around where the fee recipient is set.

content.thinking:
I found a real runtime bug in round 10 — the SubscriptionPanel is trying to divide bigint values (discountBps and feeBps) by a number, which causes a TypeError when those values are non-zero. Let me trace through how viem decodes these values to understand the exact issue.

I'm checking viem's type inference for uint16 — whether it returns a number or bigint by default. The ABI specifies discountBps as uint16, but I need to verify what type viem actually infers when decoding the tuple output from getOffering.

viem's documented behavior maps integer types ≤48 bits to `number` and larger sizes to `bigint`, so uint16 should resolve to `number`. This explains why the division `offering.discountBps / 100` typechecks without error — if discountBps were bigint, TypeScript would flag the operation as invalid. The fact that the typecheck passed confirms viem is treating it as a number at both the type and runtime level, making the Copilot comment a false positive.

That said, I could defensively wrap the division with `Number()` to handle either type and preempt any reviewer concerns — it's a cheap safeguard that works regardless of viem's version behavior and keeps the code robust.

content.thinking:
The issue is that the hardcoded fallback silently masks missing configuration in production. I need to make it fail fast by throwing an error at module load if the projectId isn't set and we're in production, while using the placeholder with a warning in development. Since this is a client component, `process.env.NODE_ENV` is available at build time, so I can check the environment and handle it appropriately—though I need to be careful about throwing during import in dev mode since that could break the entire app render.

Now I'm realizing a critical problem: during `next build`, the NODE_ENV is set to production, so if the environment variable isn't configured during the build step itself, throwing an error would cause the build to fail entirely. Since our CI runs `next build` without setting NEXT_PUBLIC_WALLETCONNECT_PROJECT_ID, this approach would break the build pipeline.

The solution is to only throw when actually running in the browser in production—checking for `typeof window !== "undefined"`—so the build phase can still succeed with a warning and fallback, while a real production browser session fails fast if the variable is missing. This way the app crashes loudly in production when it matters, but the build doesn't break. Implementing the browser-only throw approach...
